    A Pro-Life Progress Report for the 119th Congress and the Administration

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    ⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Four years ago, the Supreme Court corrected a grave legal error and overturned Roe v.
    • Industry observers note that four years ago, the Supreme Court corrected a grave legal error and overturned Roe v.
    • From appropriations to the reconciliation process, the 119th Congress protected taxpayers from supporting abortion and abortion businesses.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Four years ago, the Supreme Court corrected a grave legal error and overturned Roe v. Wade. With abortion no longer enshrined as a “right” in the Constitution, policymakers at all levels of government have stepped up to promote life in law, policy, and culture. For the first session of each newly introduced Congress, The Heritage Foundation provides pro-life policy recommendations to Members and the presidential Administration. The following year, a progress report takes stock of what has been accomplished and what remains on the to-do list. Last year, President Donald Trump and a Republican majority in Congress took the reins. Heritage provided a pro-life policy road map of ways to reverse four years of President Joe Biden’s pro-abortion radicalism.[REF] Now, this Backgrounder analyzes legislative and administrative accomplishments and highlights additional ways the Administration and Congress can protect life.In CongressFrom appropriations to the reconciliation process, the 119th Congress protected taxpayers from supporting abortion and abortion businesses.LegislationCongress advanced important legislation to promote a culture of life.Defunding Significant Abortion. Congress’s signature pro-life victory in 2025 was the One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB) budget reconciliation measure. It included a provision preventing abortion providers like Planned Parenthood from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for one year.[REF] Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s annual federal funding sources. In 2025, more than 50 clinics closed their doors, and across the country Planned Parenthood clinics are feeling the financial strain.[REF] Some blue states have stepped in to try to supplement funding but this is not sustainable in the long run.[REF] Both Planned Parenthood and blue state Attorneys General went to court to try to block the defund provision from taking effect, but were ultimately unsuccessful.[REF] Congress holds the power of the purse, and nothing in the Constitution entitles the abortion industry to Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars. As discussed below under “More to Accomplish,” another reconciliation bill could allow the defunding provision to extend beyond the OBBB’s one-year time frame, which has already passed. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF]Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Students. In January 2026, the House of Representatives passed the Pregnant Students’ Rights Act (H.R. 6359),[REF] which requires universities to provide pregnant women and girls with information about their rights, resources, and available accommodations.Pregnancy Resource Center Support. Also in January 2026, the House also passed the Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Women and Families Act (H.R. 6945),[REF] which provides statutory clarity that states can direct Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funding to pregnancy resource centers that support mothers, families, and unborn children through services like counseling, material support, and education.Addressing Weaponization and Selective Enforcement. The House Judiciary Committee approved the FACE Act Repeal Act (H.R. 589)[REF] in June 2025. The bill is needed in light of intense weaponization by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) under President Biden, which is also discussed below. The Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (FACE) Act[REF] was enacted in 1994 and prohibits physically obstructing, injuring, intimidating, or interfering with anyone “obtaining or providing reproductive health services.” Under President Biden, the DOJ deliberately targeted peaceful pro-life Americans while failing to vigorously enforce FACE Act protections that apply to churches and pregnancy centers, which faced increasing attacks following the Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. Sufficient laws already exist at the state level to address criminal activity, so Congress should repeal the FACE Act once and for all.AppropriationsCongress stood firm to protect life via spending legislation.Maintaining Status Quo of Pro-Life Policies. House-passed appropriations legislation has incorporated numerous pro-life policy riders, such as the Hyde family of amendments that prohibit taxpayer funding for abortions in foreign and domestic programs. However, new pro-life policy riders are routinely stripped during negotiations between the House and Senate.[REF]Addressing Problematic Earmarks. In FY 2024, two hospitals that perform late-term abortion procedures received almost $2.5 million in federal funds via earmarks in that year’s Labor-HHS [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services] funding.[REF] Those were Senate earmarks; the House Labor–HHS subcommittee accepted no earmark requests for FY 2024 through FY 2026.[REF] For FY 2027, the House Appropriations Committee’s Labor–HHS subcommittee provided guidance for earmark requests.[REF] Among requirements going forward, entities that perform or promote abortions are not eligible. Entities that conduct research using embryonic stem cells obtained from an induced abortion, or human germline gene modification, are not eligible. And entities that facilitate sex-rejecting interventions are not eligible.In the Trump AdministrationThe Trump Administration played a significant role in advancing pro-life policies.Previous Executive Orders and PoliciesIn 2025, the Administration swiftly acted on a host of policies, which are discussed in the 2025 Backgrounder.[REF] They include:An executive order to disentangle taxpayers from abortion funding.[REF]Reinstatement of the Protecting Life in Global Health Assistance policy, which disentangles foreign aid dollars from international nongovernmental organizations that perform or promote abortions.[REF] As discussed in the following section, the policy has since been expanded.Defunding of the United Nations Population Fund over its complicity with China’s coercive and inhumane population-control practices.[REF]Renewal of membership in the Geneva Consensus Declaration, a partnership of more than 40 countries committed to improving women’s health, protecting innocent life, and strengthening the family.[REF]Partial restoration of Title X family planning program funding to Oklahoma[REF] and Tennessee.[REF] These pro-life states were denied funding by the Biden Administration over their refusal to provide abortion counseling and referrals.Recission of a Department of Defense abortion travel policy that made travel and transportation allowances available to service members and their dependents for abortions.[REF]Rescission of Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act (EMTALA) guidance that wrongly claimed that EMTALA requires doctors to perform elective abortions.[REF]Pro-Life Regulations, Executive Orders, and Other PoliciesOver the past year and a half, the Trump Administration has taken additional steps to promote life-affirming policies. These steps include:Taxpayer Funding for Abortions. In July 2025, the Department of Justice issued an opinion[REF] that the Hyde Amendment, which prohibits taxpayer dollars from paying for elective abortions, means that the HHS cannot spend taxpayer dollars to provide “ancillary services necessary to receive an abortion”—such as the Office of Refugee Resettlement providing transportation for women seeking an abortion. The HHS has said it is reviewing the relevant regulations and guidance.[REF]Abortion in Obamacare Looks. On December 9, 2025, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) issued guidance[REF] about Section 1303 of the Affordable Care Act’s abortion coverage accounting gimmick. Section 1303 requires insurers to collect a separate payment for certain abortion coverage in qualified health plans approved to be sold on the exchanges. Maryland and other pro-abortion states attempted to commandeer excess funds remaining in abortion surcharge accounts to establish grant programs to pay for additional abortion travel and elective abortions.[REF] The CMS clarified that the leftover funds belong to insurers—not states seeking to subsidize additional abortions.As discussed below under “More to Accomplish,” the CMS should re-issue the Section 1303 regulation from President Trump’s first term. In December 2019, the CMS adopted a rule[REF] interpreting that separate payments be just that—separate—and that issuers needed to comply with the letter and spirit of Obamacare requirements. The same has not been true under Presidents Barack Obama and Biden. The CMS should rescind the Biden rule and return to the rule in place during President Trump’s first term.Abortion at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). On December 18, 2025, the DOJ issued an opinion[REF] that the Biden Administration overstepped its authority by issuing a regulation requiring abortion procedures, referrals, and counseling to veterans at VA medical facilities. The VA quickly issued a memorandum returning to pre-2022 policies that excluded abortion and abortion counseling.[REF] On December 31, the VA issued a final rule formally rescinding the 2022 Biden Administration rule that returned to the pre-2022 abortion exclusions.[REF]International Abortion Funding. In January 2026, the Trump Administration declared that it is further expanding life-affirming foreign aid policies. Since the 1980s the Mexico City Policy has required (under Republican Administrations) foreign nongovernmental organizations to certify that they will not perform or promote abortion as a condition of receiving U.S. family planning assistance. During President Trump’s first Administration, that policy was expanded to apply to more funding streams and called the Protecting Life in Global Health Assistance Policy. Now, under a new name. the Promoting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance (PHFFA) Policy has expanded to encompass abortion,[REF] radical gender ideology,[REF] and diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI)[REF] policies as well.Fetal Tissue Research. In January 2026, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) reinstated a policy from President Trump’s first term ending support for unethical and obsolete research using fetal tissue obtained from elective abortion. The prohibition applies to internal and external projects (such as grants to outside entities). [REF] The NIH can prioritize ethical alternatives instead.Planned Parenthood COVID-19 “Relief” Funding. In January 2026, the Small Business Administration (SBA) announced that it is reviewing whether Planned Parenthood affiliates improperly received more than $88 million in loans during the COVID-19 pandemic. The SBA is demanding that Planned Parenthood clinics either prove that they were eligible to receive Paycheck Protection Program loans or return the funding.[REF] During President Trump’s first term, the SBA preliminarily concluded that Planned Parenthood affiliates were not eligible to receive these loans that were meant to help small businesses, but the Biden Administration later forgave many of those loans.[REF]Department of Justice Weaponization. In April 2026, the DOJ issued an extensive report detailing how the DOJ under President Biden weaponized the FACE Act against pro-life Americans.[REF] The report concluded: (1) The DOJ violated Americans’ rights through biased enforcement; (2) the DOJ collaborated with pro-abortion organizations to track pro-life activists’ activity; (3) prosecutors repeatedly engaged in inappropriate conduct; (4) the DOJ sought harsher punishment for pro-life activists than for pro-abortion activists; and (5) the DOJ inappropriately tried to help a pro-abortion organization with an application for a grant.Reviewing Human Embryonic Stem Cell Research. In January 2026, the NIH announced a pause on submissions to the NIH Human Embryonic Stem Cell Registry and issued a request for information on ways to reduce—and potentially replace—current reliance on research using human embryonic stem cells.[REF]Pro-Life Budget Request for FY 2027. In April 2026, the Office of Management and Budget released its budget request for the upcoming fiscal year. The request includes long-standing provisions in current law, such as Hyde protections across multiple departments (foreign and domestic), conscience protections, and bioethics-related funding restrictions for certain research. Additional requests include protections separating foreign aid funding from organizations that perform or promote abortions, including additional conscience protections for medical trainees, stripping Planned Parenthood of any HHS funding, and ending funding for fetal tissue research.[REF] This proposal is a request and Congress will ultimately decide FY 2027 funding and dollar amounts. As with the FY 2026 request, the Administration demonstrated its strong commitment to pro-life policymaking throughout the government.Redirecting Teen Pregnancy Prevention Funding to Align with Pro-Family Priorities. In June 2026, the HHS canceled most federal Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program grants two years early, some of which had gone to comprehensive sex-education curricula taught by abortion providers like Planned Parenthood. The HHS opened new funding opportunities that will be available to grantees who align programming with the Administration’s priorities of sexual risk avoidance education and not encouraging, normalizing, or promoting sexual activity for minors.[REF]Conscience RightsThe Trump Administration is prioritizing enforcement of federal conscience protection laws. The HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) is ensuring that no person or organization is discriminated against over their convictions on abortion and gender ideology.In January 2026, the OCR announced a list of enforcement actions and policy changes, including:A notice of violation determining that the Illinois law requiring abortion referrals violates the Weldon and Coats–Snowe Amendments.[REF]A nationwide “Dear Colleague” letter summarizing federal health care conscience protections that the OCR is tasked with enforcing and reaffirming the Administration’s commitment to protect individuals and organizations from being discriminated against due to their sincere moral or religious convictions.[REF]Recission of Biden Administration guidance that wrongly claims that federal law on emergency medical care requires doctors to perform elective abortions.[REF]Recission of Biden Administration guidance that wrongly instructed pharmacies to stock and dispense dangerous abortion pills, even though pharmacies and pharmacists have a right to not violate their conscience by participating in abortion. Under President Biden, the HHS walked back part of this guidance after losing a court case to pharmacies challenging the guidance.[REF] Now the guidance has been rescinded entirely.[REF]Disavowal of[REF] the Biden Administration’s August 2021 decision to withdraw the Trump Administration’s 2020 Notice of Violation that California broke federal conscience rights law over its insurance coverage mandate for elective abortion.Disavowal of[REF] the Biden Administration’s July 2021 decision to withdraw the Trump Administration’s Notice of Violation that the University of Vermont Medical Center broke federal conscience rights law by requiring a health care professional to participate in an abortion procedure despite strong objection.In March 2026, the HHS announced that the OCR is investigating 13 states over possible violations of the Weldon Amendment, which claims government cannot discriminate against health care entities that do not pay for or provide coverage of abortions.[REF] The states under investigation have abortion coverage requirements for plans sold in their respective jurisdictions.[REF]In May 2026, the HHS announced an additional reorganization within the OCR.[REF] The OCR is tasked with enforcing federal civil rights laws related to conscience, religious freedom, privacy, cybersecurity, and more. In 2018, during President Trump’s first term, the HHS created a Conscience and Religious Freedom Division within the OCR. Under President Biden, this division was shuttered and absorbed, with the Civil Rights Division, into the Policy Division.[REF] Rights of conscience and religious freedom are not “less than.” Restoring the Conscience and Religious Freedom Division will provide the OCR with the tools it needs to best serve all Americans and ensure that their fundamental rights are respected.More to AccomplishBoth Congress and the Administration have successfully advanced important pro-life policies, but there is still more work to do.In CongressDefunding Big Abortion, maintaining long-standing pro-life policy riders, and holding bad actors accountable must continue to be a priority.Planned Parenthood. Preventing Planned Parenthood and other abortion providers from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for one year was a signature accomplishment in the 2025 OBBB budget reconciliation package. Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s federal funding sources. However, this defunding provision was the only one in the entire bill subject to a one-year time frame rather than the full 10 years to which the bill can apply. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF] If Congress discusses another reconciliation bill, the defunding provision should be incorporated for the full 10-year time frame so that taxpayers do not have to continue funding abortion providers.Appropriations. Congress has continued to include long-standing riders like the Hyde Amendment and similar language in annual appropriations bills, prohibiting taxpayer dollars from paying for most abortions. But many other pro-life policies can be enacted via appropriations riders. From expanding conscience protections to reinstating commonsense safety protections for risky abortion pills, there is more that Congress should do to promote life in must-pass spending legislation.[REF]Oversight. Congress should continue to invoke its oversight and investigatory role to hold bad actors accountable and ensure that that pro-life priorities in the Administration are not sidelined. For example, in 2022, activists obtained the remains of five preemie-size unborn babies who had been aborted at a notorious Washington, DC, late-term abortion mill. According to expert testimony, these babies may have been aborted using the illegal partial-birth abortion technique. One baby was still in the amniotic sac and may have been born alive and left to die.[REF] Local authorities stonewalled questions from Congress and the press about any investigation of this activity. Pro-life activists and Members of Congress feared that the DC Office of the Chief Medical Examiner would destroy the five bodies, but in February 2024 it confirmed that it would not immediately do so.[REF] During a June 2025 hearing, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi indicated that there was an ongoing investigation.[REF]Demand FDA Action on Dangerous Abortion Drugs. Congress should continue demanding transparency from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on its long-promised comprehensive review of the abortion pill. It is abundantly clear that current FDA postmarketing safety policies are not adequately protecting women and children.[REF] In light of the politicized approval process that put this risky drug on the market in the first place, a complete and thorough review is long overdue. Leadership changes at the FDA should not slow down or deprioritize this important work. Individual members and congressional committees should continue emphasizing the dangers these drugs pose to women, girls, and unborn children.In the Trump AdministrationThe Trump Administration should rescind Biden-era regulations and policies that promoted abortion and sought to undermine the 2022 Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. These include:Abortion Travel for Unaccompanied Illegal Alien Children (UACs). A senior Office of Refugee Resettlement official told The Daily Signal[REF] that the agency is working on reversing a Biden-era regulation allowing taxpayer-funded abortion travel for UACs.[REF] The changes were submitted to the Office of Management and Budget’s Regulatory Information Service Center in January 2026, but the updated regulation has not been formally proposed yet. Section 1303 also requires issuers to collect a separate payment from each enrollee for the abortion coverage portion and segregate those funds in separate allocation accounts solely used for abortion coverage. Plans are also required to provide notice to enrollees at the time of enrollment that the strategy includes abortion coverage.     Industry observers note that four years ago, the Supreme Court corrected a grave legal error and overturned Roe v. Wade. With abortion no longer enshrined as a “right” in the Constitution, policymakers at all levels of government have stepped up to promote life in law, policy, and culture. For the first session of each latest Congress, The Heritage Foundation provides pro-life policy recommendations to Members and the presidential Administration. The following year, a progress report takes stock of what has been accomplished and what remains on the to-do list. Last year, President Donald Trump and a Republican majority in Congress took the reins. Heritage provided a pro-life policy road map of ways to reverse four years of President Joe Biden’s pro-abortion radicalism.[REF] Now, this Backgrounder analyzes legislative and administrative accomplishments and highlights additional ways the Administration and Congress can protect life.

    From appropriations to the reconciliation process, the 119th Congress protected taxpayers from supporting abortion and abortion businesses.

    Congress advanced important legislation to promote a culture of life.

It included a provision preventing abortion providers like Planned Parenthood from receiving Medicaid reimbursements for one year.[REF] Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s annual federal funding sources. In 2025, more than 50 clinics closed their doors, and across the country Planned Parenthood clinics are feeling the financial strain.[REF] Some blue states have stepped in to try to supplement funding but this is not sustainable in the long run.[REF] Both Planned Parenthood and blue state Attorneys General went to court to try to block the defund provision from taking effect, but were ultimately unsuccessful.[REF] Congress holds the power of the purse, and nothing in the Constitution entitles the abortion industry to Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars. As discussed below under “More to Accomplish,” another reconciliation bill could allow the defunding provision to extend beyond the OBBB’s one-year time frame, which has already passed. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF].

    Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Students. In January 2026, the House of Representatives passed the Pregnant Students’ Rights Act (H.R. 6359),[REF] which requires universities to provide pregnant women and girls with information about their rights, resources, and available accommodations.

    Pregnancy Resource Center Support. Also in January 2026, the House also passed the Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Women and Families Act (H.R. 6945),[REF] which provides statutory clarity that states can direct Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) funding to pregnancy resource centers that support mothers, families, and unborn children through services like counseling, material support, and education.

    It has been revealed that addressing Weaponization and Selective Enforcement. The House Judiciary Committee approved the FACE Act Repeal Act (H.R. 589)[REF] in June 2025. The bill is needed in light of intense weaponization by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) under President Biden, which is also discussed below. The Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (FACE) Act[REF] was enacted in 1994 and prohibits physically obstructing, injuring, intimidating, or interfering with anyone “obtaining or providing reproductive health services.” Under President Biden, the DOJ deliberately targeted peaceful pro-life Americans while failing to vigorously enforce FACE Act protections that apply to churches and pregnancy centers, which faced increasing attacks following the Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade. Sufficient laws already exist at the state level to address criminal activity, so Congress should repeal the FACE Act once and for all.

    Congress stood firm to protect life via spending legislation.

    Sources indicate that maintaining Status Quo of Pro-Life Policies. House-passed appropriations legislation has incorporated numerous pro-life policy riders, such as the Hyde family of amendments that prohibit taxpayer funding for abortions in foreign and domestic programs. However, newly introduced pro-life policy riders are routinely stripped during negotiations between the House and Senate.[REF].

    Addressing Problematic Earmarks. In FY 2024, two hospitals that perform late-term abortion procedures received almost $2.5 million in federal funds via earmarks in that year’s Labor-HHS [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services] funding.[REF] Those were Senate earmarks; the House Labor–HHS subcommittee accepted no earmark requests for FY 2024 through FY 2026.[REF] For FY 2027, the House Appropriations Committee’s Labor–HHS subcommittee provided guidance for earmark requests.[REF] Among requirements going forward, entities that perform or promote abortions are not eligible. Entities that conduct research using embryonic stem cells obtained from an induced abortion, or human germline gene modification, are not eligible. And entities that facilitate sex-rejecting interventions are not eligible.

    In January 2026, the OCR announced a list of enforcement actions and policy changes, including:.

    According to recent reports, in May 2026, the HHS announced an additional reorganization within the OCR.[REF] The OCR is tasked with enforcing federal civil rights laws related to conscience, religious freedom, privacy, cybersecurity, and more. In 2018, during President Trump’s first term, the HHS created a Conscience and Religious Freedom Division within the OCR. Under President Biden, this division was shuttered and absorbed, with the Civil Rights Division, into the Policy Division.[REF] Rights of conscience and religious freedom are not “less than.” Restoring the Conscience and Religious Freedom Division will provide the OCR with the tools it needs to best serve all Americans and ensure that their fundamental rights are respected.

    Both Congress and the Administration have successfully advanced key pro-life policies, but there is still more work to do.

    Defunding Significant Abortion, maintaining long-standing pro-life policy riders, and holding bad actors accountable must continue to be a priority.

    Recent findings suggest that planned Parenthood. Medicaid makes up most of Planned Parenthood’s federal funding sources. However, this defunding provision was the only one in the entire bill subject to a one-year time frame rather than the full 10 years to which the bill can apply. Planned Parenthood and other large abortion providers became eligible to receive Medicaid funds again on July 4, 2026.[REF] If Congress discusses another reconciliation bill, the defunding provision should be incorporated for the full 10-year time frame so that taxpayers do not have to continue funding abortion providers.

But many other pro-life policies can be enacted via appropriations riders. From expanding conscience protections to reinstating commonsense safety protections for risky abortion pills, there is more that Congress should do to promote life in must-pass spending legislation.[REF].

    In a recent development, demand FDA Action on Dangerous Abortion Drugs. It is abundantly clear that current FDA postmarketing safety policies are not adequately protecting women and children.[REF] In light of the politicized approval process that put this risky drug on the market in the first place, a complete and thorough review is long overdue. Leadership changes at the FDA should not slow down or deprioritize this important work. Individual members and congressional committees should continue emphasizing the dangers these drugs pose to women, girls, and unborn children.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    Most AE roles ask you to sell a product you only half understand to buyers who already know they want it. This is not that role. You'll sell a deeply technical product to developers, CTOs, and product teams — people who can smell a script from a mile away and will respect you more for going deep on the tech than for any closing line you've practiced. We don't have a polished playbook handed down from a head of sales who left three companies ago. We have a upcoming sales leader, a market that's exploding faster than we can keep up with, and a real opportunity for the right person to help define the motion from the inside.

    If you're energized by ambiguity, allergic to bureaucracy, and the kind of seller who genuinely enjoys learning why a customer is building what they're building — keep reading.

    You'll thrive as an Account Executive if you:.

    are obsessed with making the best product for our customers.

    are known as the go-to person for tackling tough problems.

    work hard and can build and ship fast.

    are focused on polish, detail and quality.

    are a fast learner, frequently picking up fresh tips, tricks, and skills.

    The best way to impress us is with thoughtful ways you'd implement LiveKit, and potentially tinkering with it 😊.

    Own and manage the full sales cycle, from prospecting and discovery to demos, negotiation, and close.

    Develop deep product understanding and communicate technical value to developers, CTOs, and product teams.

    Generate pipeline through outbound efforts and strategic partnerships, with support from marketing and sales development.

    Build and maintain strong relationships with prospects and customers, identifying their goals and how our platform helps them succeed.

    Collaborate with Product and Engineering to bring customer feedback into roadmap discussions and positioning.

    Help shape and evolve our sales playbook, messaging, and GTM motion as one of the earliest sales hires.

    Accurately forecast and track pipeline activity, working closely with leadership to inform strategy and planning.

    4+ years of full-cycle SaaS sales experience, with at least 2 of those years selling into enterprise.

    A track record of consistently selling 6-figure deals and hitting or exceeding quota in fast-paced or early-stage environments.

    Strong instincts for selling technical products — APIs, developer tools, or infrastructure tooling — you don't shy away from going deep with technical buyers.

    Comfortable in low-process, high-autonomy environments and bringing structure where it's missing.

    Able to translate technical capability into business value for both technical buyers and executive stakeholders.

    High accountability, ownership, and bias for action — you don't wait to be told what the right next move is.

    Disciplined with CRM and pipeline hygiene (HubSpot, Salesforce, etc.).

    Experience selling at an infrastructure or developer-tools manufacturer, ideally with multi-product or platform sales motion.

    Time spent as one of the earliest sellers at a startup — you know what it feels like to build the plane while flying it.

    A real interest in voice AI, agents, or real-time infrastructure (not just "AI" in your LinkedIn headline).

    You once spent a Saturday building something with an API just to see if you could 😏.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    It has been revealed that liveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • appellate decision Thursday in Att'y Grievance Comm.
    • It has been revealed that the motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of Latest York on September 29, 2025.
    • It has been revealed that on September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the New York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From a N.Y. appellate decision Thursday in Att'y Grievance Comm. v. Fernich (Judges Sallie Manzanet-Daniels, Tanya R. Kennedy, Barbara R. Kapnick, Kelly O'Neill Levy, and Matthew Parker-Raso); the respondent, Marc Fernich, is a prominent Newly introduced York criminal defense lawyer, who represented, among others, Jeffrey Epstein, John Gotti, and Joaquin Guzman (drug cartel leader El Chapo):.

    It has been revealed that the motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of Latest York on September 29, 2025. On May 27, 2026, the AGC served respondent with a notice and petition of charges alleging one charge of professional misconduct under Rules of Professional Misconduct (22 NYCRR 1200.0) rule 8.4(h), which prohibits conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's fitness as a lawyer. The parties have submitted a stipulation of facts, respondent's affidavit, and materials addressing aggravation and mitigation. Respondent admits to the stipulated misconduct, acknowledges the consequences of consenting to discipline, and agrees to a public censure.

    It has been revealed that on September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the New York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge. On Centre Street, he came upon a group of demonstrators in support of Palestine outside of the federal courthouse. Some demonstrators were singing and chanting, one played a guitar, and others held a banner reading "Jewish Artists for Palestine.".

    Respondent attempted to make his way through a circle of demonstrators, and admits that physical contact occurred as he attempted to proceed. Respondent grabbed a demonstrator's arm, pushed and grabbed others while moving through the circle, and engaged in heated verbal confrontation. The cellphone recordings of the incident also show respondent holding a demonstrator from behind with his arms around the person's waist, with the demonstrator shouting at him to remove his arms, respondent pushing and grabbing others, and respondent holding another demonstrator from behind with his arms around the individual's neck.

    Sources indicate that among other things, respondent's threatening and antisemitic remarks included "Back off me, Kapo, Kike, Jew Boy!," "You fucking animal, you're worse than a fucking Muslim!," "You should have been aborted," and "You should have been thrown into an oven, I'd throw you in if I could!" He also said that the demonstrators' grandparents should have died in the Holocaust, as well as other inflammatory remarks invoking violence. Respondent remained at the demonstration for approximately one hour, until it ended.

    At his deposition, respondent maintained that the video depiction of the incident was a compilation of cellphone recordings made by several individuals and that they were out of sequence and out of context. He asserted that the confrontation had not been one-sided; demonstrators had been linking arms, blocking his way, pushing back, and squeezing his genitals.

    He also maintained that the recordings had purposefully omitted much of the physical contact and extreme anti-Israel and anti-Zionist rhetoric directed at him. Nonetheless, he recognized that the demonstrators had been exercising their constitutional rights to assemble and engage in free speech, and that his words and actions could not be justified. He was deeply ashamed of his conduct and expressed remorse.

    The parties have stipulated that respondent's misconduct is aggravated by his substantial experience in the practice of law. They have also stipulated to considerable mitigation. Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. The incident was unrelated to his representation of a client or the practice of law, and did not disrupt a court proceeding. Respondent self-reported his misconduct to the AGC through counsel, cooperated with the AGC investigation, voluntarily appeared for examination, accepted responsibility, and expressed remorse and embarrassment for his actions. Fifteen character references described respondent as being well-regarded in the community and having character traits of honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness.

    The record further reflects that respondent was experiencing significant medical problems at the time of the incident. He was recovering from a recent back surgery and experiencing significant pain, and had undergone emergency surgery for retinal tears shortly beforehand. He was also undergoing psychiatric treatment and taking medication for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. A report submitted by respondent's treating psychiatrist explains how the pain, emotional distress, and psychiatric symptoms respondent was experiencing may have contributed to his impaired judgment and agitation and, while respondent had been under his care for 13 years, he would never have expected him to engage in the kind of "angry and out-of-control conduct that he engaged in outside the Courthouse." Respondent, who has family in Israel, also maintains that the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel affected him deeply and that his memory of those attacks caused his anger to boil over.

    Sources indicate that under 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5), the Court may resolve a disciplinary matter by consent where the submissions establish an admitted violation and an appropriate agreed-upon sanction. In support of the proposal for a public censure, the parties cite decisions imposing a censure for similarly offensive, abusive, and discriminatory remarks and other isolated misconduct (see e.g. Matter of Melogy, 233 AD3d 135 [1st Dept 2024]; Matter of Mukambetova, 204 AD3d 158 [1st Dept 2022]; Matter of Schlossberg, 192 AD3d 8 [1st Dept 2020]).

    In a recent development, respondent's use of antisemitic and threatening language, together with his physical aggression towards demonstrators, warrants public discipline. At the same time, the absence of a disciplinary history, the isolated nature of the incident, the medical and psychological circumstances, his cooperation, and his acceptance of responsibility supports the sanction jointly proposed. Public censure appropriately expresses the profession's condemnation of the relevant conduct while also recognizing the substantial mitigation.

    Accordingly, the parties' joint motion for discipline by consent pursuant to 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5) should be granted, … and respondent publicly censured….

    Jorge Dopico and Raymond Vallejo represent the Committee.

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service.
    • According to recent reports, veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service.
    • Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, veterans Day is more than a commemoration of military service. It is also a reminder that freedom depends on citizens willing to serve something larger than themselves—and not just when they are in uniform.Our service members do much more than most of us realize, and our society is the better for it.Across generations, American veterans have answered the nation’s call in war and peace out of a commitment to duty, sacrifice and country. Their example shows that citizenship carries responsibilities as well as rights, and that self-government endures only when citizens place the common good above personal interest.The freedoms that Americans enjoy today were secured by all veterans who served. They defended not merely our borders but also the principles upon which this nation was founded: liberty, representative government and the rule of law.By defending the constitutional order, veterans helped preserve a nation in which political differences are settled through lawful debate and elections rather than force. Veterans Day is an opportunity to recognize the men and women whose sacrifices have made that peaceful self-government possible.>>> The Three Values That Are the Real Keys to America’s GreatnessVeterans have helped secure liberty against some of the most oppressive ideologies in human history, including communism and national socialism. American veterans were instrumental in defeating the Nazi regime during World War II, helping liberate Europe from a government built on tyranny, aggression and the systematic denial of human freedom.During the Cold War, generations of American servicemen and women stood watch against the expansion of Soviet communism, preserving the security of the free world through deterrence and steadfast resolve. Their service helped create the conditions that led to the collapse of the Soviet Union and the liberation of millions of people in Central and Eastern Europe.The freedom enjoyed today by nations once trapped behind the Iron Curtain is part of the legacy of those veterans who answered their country’s call.Across these conflicts, American veterans served as guardians of the principle that free people have the right to govern themselves. Veterans Day also reminds us that liberty is never self-executing. The constitutional freedoms secured through military sacrifice endure only when citizens practice the discipline, responsibility and respect for law that self-government requires.The veteran’s example therefore reaches beyond the battlefield, offering a model for preserving freedom in civic life.Veterans also participate in freedom’s defense at home at some of the highest rates in American society. According to the 2025 Veterans Civic Health Index, 81% of veterans were registered to vote in the 2024 election, compared with 74% of nonveterans. Specifically, plaintiffs contend that their complaints state causes of action for products liability based on defective features of these social media defendants' platforms and their failure to warn thereof….

    In a recent development, [P]laintiffs failed to adequately plead that features of [the] social media defendants' products proximately caused their injuries. Generally, a defendant's acts qualify as a proximate cause when they are "a substantial cause of the events which produced the injury." This inquiry examines.

    "the foreseeability of the event resulting in injury; the passage of time between the originally negligent act and the intervening act; the spatial gap, if any, between the original act and the intervening act; whether the original act of negligence was a completed occurrence or was ongoing at the time of the intervening act; whether and, if so, what other forces combined to bring about the harm; as well as public policy considerations regarding the scope of liability.".

    In a recent development, foreseeability is often the most significant factor. Indeed, if an unforeseeable intervening criminal act of a third party causes the plaintiff's injury, the causal connection is severed. Thus, proximate causation will not be found when the intervening act "is extraordinary under the circumstances, not foreseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of or far removed from the defendant's conduct." "Although foreseeability and proximate cause are generally questions for the factfinder, there are instances in which proximate cause can be determined as a matter of law because 'only one conclusion may be drawn from the established facts'" such as when "the original negligent act merely 'furnished the occasion for'—but did not cause—'an unrelated act to cause injuries not ordinarily anticipated.'".

    Here, plaintiffs failed to adequately allege that the remaining social media defendants' product defects proximately caused the shooter to carry out the mass shooting that resulted in plaintiffs' injuries. The complaints, even accepting the factual allegations as true, fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants' decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.

    Sources indicate that instead, under the circumstances, the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. {Our conclusion is limited to the unusual facts of this case, where the platforms' assertedly addictive features were alleged to have harmed the shooter rather than the plaintiffs directly.} We therefore need not address the scope of section 230 of the Communications Decency Act or how it would apply to the claims against these defendants.

    Judge Halligan joined the majority, but also wrote a concurring opinion:.

    I join the majority because I agree that the plaintiffs have not adequately pleaded proximate causation. I write separately to underscore that, for me, this conclusion rests squarely on the highly unusual facts presented here, and to offer some additional thoughts regarding the scope of section 230.

    Industry observers note that as an initial matter, I agree with my dissenting colleagues that the plaintiffs alleged that several of the defendants tortiously designed addictive products. The complaints make a number of general claims about social media and youth: that defendants' platforms are addictive; that compulsive use of social media, particularly by young people, causes emotional disturbance and "impulsive decision-making and risk-taking behavior"; and that such use can also yield other deleterious consequences, including "sleep disturbances, mental health problems and suicidal ideation, and violent, hateful acts." The complaints further assert that the social media defendants, knowing of the addictive quality of their products and the heightened susceptibility of young consumers, not only failed to implement features for limiting use or warning parents, but also took deliberate advantage of that vulnerability by utilizing "strategic timing and clustering of notifications to lure back users" and by implementing "barriers to the deactivation and deletion of accounts." ….

    I find the claims before us quite distinct from the cases cited by the dissent that have allowed products liability claims premised on the addictiveness of social media platforms to proceed. I have little doubt that a plaintiff could allege a sufficient connection between the design of a platform and adverse consequences for the mental health of young users. In those cases, the harms that form the basis for the claims—for example, the alleged inducement of "compulsive use among young users to the detriment of their health and well-being"—flow directly from the platforms' allegedly defective features, leaving little question "that the defective design was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff's injury.".

    According to recent reports, but the plaintiffs here are not bringing a claim on behalf of users. Instead, they are seeking recompense for the victims of a crime committed by a social media user. In other words, the allegedly addictive properties of the platforms were not alleged to have harmed the plaintiffs here directly, but rather to have harmed the shooter, who in turn engaged in extensive research and planning before murdering ten people and wounding others…. I do not see the connection between the two as sufficiently articulated to allow the case to proceed.

    Three aspects of these claims inform my conclusion. First, although intervening criminal acts do not necessarily sever the causal chain, the shooter's conduct was apparently painstakingly planned and extraordinarily violent.

    Second, the prominence of content in many of plaintiffs' allegations gives me real pause. Even if we were to interpret section 230 as not immunizing defendants against claims for actions that rest, at least in part, on content, I am not aware of other instances where a court has held that provocative content proximately caused someone to commit a violent crime, and I am hesitant to take that step here. {I understand the plaintiffs to disclaim on appeal any effort to base liability on defendants' roles as publishers of content. But their complaints can be read to allege that the platforms are defective at least in part because of the racist and extremist content they make available, and the plaintiffs acknowledge that content is a necessary link in the causal chain leading to their harms.}.

    Third, the defendants' platforms have billions of worldwide users. To the extent that proximate cause could rest on a correlation between social media use and a specific type of harmful act committed by any one of those users, the potential liability would sweep broadly, to say the least. If all such conduct were "a natural and foreseeable consequence" of a platform's design choices, the concept of proximate cause would have little meaning….

    As for section 230, …. "we [have] read section 230 to bar 'lawsuits seeking to hold a service provider liable for its exercise of a publisher's traditional editorial functions.'" … Our endorsement of a "traditional editorial functions" test for section 230 immunity, however, does little to answer whether the conduct of modern social media platforms can be labelled such a function.

    In a recent development, as to claims that a defendant designed its platform features to encourage or facilitate addiction, irrespective of the particular content promoted by the platform, I agree with the dissent that they are not barred by section 230. That is because such conduct does not constitute a traditional editorial function, even under a broad understanding of that term.

    As to claims that challenge a social media platform's use of content-recommendation algorithms, the dissent appears to take the view that content-recommendation algorithms which are designed to be addictive are not covered by section 230 immunity, since they increase engagement in a way that could not have been envisioned at the time that provision was enacted in 1996. I have no quarrel with how we framed the scope of section 230 in Shiamili: the key question is whether a platform engaged in a traditional editorial function, akin to a decision "to publish, withdraw, postpone or alter content." But whether platforms' use of content-recommendation algorithms can be stated to resemble traditional decisions to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content is, for me, a more difficult question….

    [O]verly broad interpretations of section 230 in the face of a rapidly changing technological landscape are unmoored from Congress's purpose in enacting that provision—to protect minors from being exposed to pornography online…. Given that caution, I would not be inclined to extend section 230's reach to all content-recommendation algorithms. I am particularly skeptical that use of individualized content-recommendation algorithms—that is, algorithms that "assess[ ] a user's prior posts, friends, or viewing habits to recommend fresh content and connections"—constitutes a traditional publisher function. After all, "[t]raditional publication has never included selecting the news, opinion pieces, or classified ads to send to each individual reader based on guesses as to their preferences and interests." Instead, such functions may be "more analogous to the actions of a direct marketer, matchmaker, or recruiter than to those of a publisher.".

    In my view, a closer question is presented as to engagement-maximizing algorithms that, unlike the algorithms described above, do not take into account any individual user's conduct but instead seek to "promote[ ] third-party content" based on "cumulative user engagement." On one hand, algorithms that do not respond to individual user conduct may be thought to resemble a publisher's traditional aim of presenting content that users, on the whole, want to see. On the other hand, one might conclude that "generic" content-based algorithms bear no more resemblance to traditional publication than their "'advanced'—individualized—counterparts" because they still rely on an assessment of user viewing habits in a manner akin to "a direct marketer" rather than a traditional publisher. My dissenting colleagues offer yet another variation on this point; they assert that engagement-maximizing algorithms differ from an editor's choice of where to place a news story because the algorithms are "designed to prey on neurological frailties and alter brain chemistry.".

    In a recent development, whether section 230 protects any of these algorithms is, for me, a difficult question, and I do not think the record before us sheds much light on how different types of content-recommendation algorithms actually operate on the social media defendants' individual platforms—information that might affect my view. We need not decide those questions today because, whatever the scope of the "traditional editorial functions" protected by section 230, the plaintiffs have failed to sufficiently allege that the defendants' platforms' features caused their grave injuries.

    Judge Rivera, joined by Chief Judge Wilson and Judge Troutman, dissented in relevant part; an excerpt from the very long opinion:.

    The complaints detail the shooter's transformation from a seemingly ordinary teenager into a virulent racist and violent white supremacist…. [In his manifesto, t]he shooter also wrote that he "was not born racist nor [did he] gr[o]w up to be racist." Rather, he was exposed to and indoctrinated in his ideology of racial violence after using various social media platforms, starting with Instagram, YouTube, and Snapchat in his early teen years, before he transitioned to more niche platforms like Reddit, Discord, Twitch and 4chan. The shooter claimed he swiftly "became transfixed with and addicted to [the] online world." He wrote in his diary:.

    "I'm addict[ed] to consoooooming. It's 2 in the morning. w[hat] t[he] f[*ck] … I'll admit my mental health has seriously degraded these past few years, especially in the last few months. I should be sleeping right now. I'm just browsing online:/" (emphasis added).

    By his own account, he sacrificed "years of [his] life" to being online, often "stay[ing] up late" "browsing Reddit or watching YouTube" "every day." He stated that his compulsive social media use "seriously degraded" his mental health and isolated him from his peers. Rather than "go[ing] to friend's houses" or other social gatherings, "[e]very day after school [he] would just go home and play games and watch YouTube, mostly by [him]self." Ultimately, as he descended further into isolation, he believed he had no other choice but to commit this barbarous act.

    Sources indicate that plaintiffs allege that the shooter's experience of compulsive social media engagement is widespread because the products' addictive features are fundamental to the social media defendants' business model. According to plaintiffs, defendants' business models seek to maximize user engagement through products "designed to be addictive." Plaintiffs assert that the operation of these products on the shooter, and their adverse impact on his mind caused by their addictive features, are links in the proximate causal chain underlying plaintiffs' tort liability causes of action against the social media defendants….

    In a recent development, the Appellate Division erroneously concluded that defendants are immune from plaintiffs' lawsuit under Section 230. As I discuss, Section 230 does not shield defendants from plaintiffs' products liability and failure to warn allegations grounded on allegedly addictive products, as those claims have nothing to do with defendants' role as a third-party content publisher or as the creator of protected speech….

    To the extent plaintiffs' claims against the social media defendants are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content, including racist, white supremacist, and violent content, defendants are immune from suit pursuant to Section 230. However, not all claims asserted in the complaints are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content. Rather, as I explain, the complaints also stated causes of action based on defendants' design of allegedly defective products and failure to warn….

    Plaintiffs assert that these defendants are civilly liable for their role in addicting the shooter to social media and consequent deterioration of his mental health. Plaintiffs' complaints set forth the entire chain of causation that allegedly led to the mass shooting. By designing highly addictive algorithms known to cause severe mental harm to teenagers—like the shooter—the social media defendants created a direct link to the resulting damages, particularly given their failure to warn people and parents of these risks…. [T]here is no Section 230 immunity that attaches to the architecture of defendants' social media products—particularly their purposefully addictive algorithms….

    In a recent development, defendants' alternative argument that the complaints were properly dismissed on First Amendment grounds is unpersuasive. At this pre-answer stage of the litigation, it is unclear how precisely the content-recommendation algorithms function, meaning it is not possible to determine, as a matter of law, on a motion to dismiss that the algorithms themselves are protected speech. That determination requires factual findings dependent on future discovery. On a motion to dismiss we only decide whether the plaintiffs' claim is cognizable and not whether it will eventually succeed based on the facts established by the record….

    And here's a short excerpt from the dissent's long discussion of why it rejects the majority's proximate cause theory:.

    It has been revealed that the majority's conclusion that plaintiffs "fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence" of the social media defendants' platforms because "the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law" is unsupported by our well-established tort liability doctrines. First, we have made clear that there may be more than one link in a causal chain and there may be more than one tortfeasor liable, jointly or individually, for a plaintiff's injuries. "[T]he mere fact that other persons share some responsibility for [the] plaintiff's harm does not absolve [a] defendant from liability." Thus, the fact that the third-party content creators may bear responsibility for the harm does not mean that defendants bear none.

    In a recent development, second, a defect need only be a "substantial cause"—not the sole cause—"of the events which produced the injury." Substantial means more than slight or trivial. Plaintiffs' allegations that defendants' product adversely affected the shooter's mental health and behavior, making him a compulsive social media user, with the attendant negative impact on his mind and body, isolated from others, rendering him more susceptible to commit this horrific violent act, easily satisfies the "substantial cause" standard.

    Third, not all intervening acts break the causal chain. An intervening act only breaks the causal nexus if it is extraordinary under the circumstances, unforeseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of and far removed from the defendant's conduct. That determination depends on whether the intervening act and its consequences were the foreseeable result of a defendant's tortious conduct. Even the "intentional" or "criminal" intervening acts of a third party can be reasonably foreseeable….

    [W]hile here, the harm arose from exposure to graphic violence and white supremacist propaganda, plaintiffs allege that the algorithm is content-agnostic. According to plaintiffs, defendants' products and platforms rely on these complex algorithms to keep consumers engaged, which negatively impacts young people's mental health, and, in turn, increases the tendency to violent behavior, all the while driving revenue for these defendants. Thus, the majority's assertion that the shooter's actions were not foreseeable is nothing more than a factual conclusion, but that determination cannot be made by the Court on a motion to dismiss….

    Eric A. Shumsky, Moez M. Kaba, and Lisa LeCours are listed as representing the platforms.

    My forthcoming chapter on "Emergency Powers" is now available on SSRN. It is coauthored with Josh Braver (University of Wisconsin), and will be published in the forthcoming Cato Handbook on Executive Power, edited by Molly Nixon. Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these challenges, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:.

    Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

    Industry observers note that this chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of latest legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

    I recently covered related issues in an article for Just Security, which goes over potential legislative reforms. In the Cato Handbook chapter, Braver and I cover both legislative reforms and how judicial review can be strengthened.

    Breaking: Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (448 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that from today's decision in U.S.
    • Recent findings suggest that [W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met.
    • It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing fresh terms for future cooperation in any event….
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that from today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:.

    Recent findings suggest that [W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed newly introduced limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

    It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing fresh terms for future cooperation in any event….

    [But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a new state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "matter orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

    Our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

    Recent findings suggest that we also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

    Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

    Judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

    District attorneys and victims’ families have taken their fight to the California Supreme Court over California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s strategy to commute over 500 death row penalty sentences.

    Newsom, who has served two terms, declared a moratorium on all executions in 2019 and leaves office in January.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As world leaders recently gathered in Phnom Penh to celebrate the 20th Francophonie Summit with the theme of peace and shared prosperity, French President Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to call publicly for an investigation into the killing of former Cambodian lawmaker and French citizen Lim Kimya. It was a rare public rebuke of the Cambodian government by a foreign leader.

    A gunman killed Kimya in Bangkok, Thailand in January 2025. Kimya had served as a parliament member with the opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party before its 2017 dissolution.

    According to recent reports, A Thai court convicted the gunman, Ekkalak Paenoi, in October 2025 and issued arrest warrants for two Cambodian suspects, Ly Ratanakraksmey and Pich Kimsrin, both of whom have connections to high-ranking Cambodian officials. The Cambodian government—like many of its neighbors in Southeast Asia—is increasingly persecuting activists abroad.

    The Cambodian government has yet to acknowledge the arrest warrants or start an impartial investigation. Both men remain at large. France has issued Interpol Red Notices for them on charges of complicity in premeditated murder.

    It has been revealed that macron’s raising Kimya’s murder during a joint press conference with Prime Minister Hun Manet sends a strong message that the French government is taking Cambodian authorities’ attacks on activists abroad seriously. The Cambodian government should heed the call and independently and impartially investigate the murder.

    It has been revealed that but political repression by the Cambodian government runs deeper than one case. Ahead of 2027 local elections, the authorities are escalating their crackdown on the long suppressed political opposition. Young activists in particular, such as the five imprisoned Mother Nature Cambodia environmental activists, have been punished with baseless treason charges and lengthy prison sentences. Concerned governments should publicly and privately urge Cambodian authorities to release the more than 100 Cambodians currently imprisoned for exercising their fundamental freedoms.

    Human Rights Watch was among the local and international organizations that pressed Cambodian authorities to release the Mother Nature activists and others ahead of the Francophonie Summit. The ruling Cambodian People’s Party, which exerts complete control over the country’s courts, was apparently unbothered by these efforts.

    Other foreign leaders should amplify Macron’s message and publicly call on Cambodia’s government to reopen the space for the political opposition and respect the fundamental rights of all Cambodians, both at home and abroad.

    Journalists, activists and political opponents who fled Burkina Faso to escape the junta’s repression now risk arrest and prosecution abroad, as the country’s judicial authorities pursue dozens of individuals over alleged terrorism-related offenses.

    Burkina Faso Prosecutor General Désiré Sawadogo revealed on November 13 that a special court handling terrorism-related offenses had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities. All those targeted exposed serious military abuses during counterinsurgency operations and include exiled journalists critical of the junta, among them Ahmed Newton Barry, Issaka Lingani, Inoussa Ouédraogo, Adama Ouedraogo, and Abdoulaye Barry; exiled social media activist Naïm Touré; former foreign affairs minister Alpha Barry, and international journalist Wassim Nasr. They face various charges, including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism.

    It has been revealed that burkina Faso sent international arrest warrants and extradition requests to Côte d’Ivoire, France, and the United States, mentioned Sawadogo. He added that Burkina Faso asked the United States to use Meta to identify and prosecute Facebook page administrators accused of promoting terrorism.

    The authorities are using counterterrorism laws to target critical voices and restrict independent reporting on military abuses. The extradition requests extend political repression beyond Burkina Faso’s borders, placing critics who sought protection abroad at risk of arrest, forced return, and further abuse. The government’s recent decision to reinstate capital punishment for offenses including terrorism, high treason, and espionage is also of grave concern.

    Since seizing power in a September 2022 coup, the junta has restricted fundamental rights through media bans, suspension of unions and civil society organizations, dissolution of political parties, enforced disappearances, and the unlawful conscription of government critics.

    Meanwhile, the conflict between government forces and allied militias and Islamist armed groups, ongoing since 2017, has involved widespread abuses by all parties, including war crimes and crimes against humanity, with no accountability. Human Rights Watch has documented serious flaws in the special terrorism court, including prolonged pretrial detention, and violations of fair trial guarantees.

    Concerned governments should rigorously scrutinize all extradition and judicial cooperation requests from Burkina Faso. No journalist, activist or political opponent should be returned where there are substantial grounds to fear torture, arbitrary detention, an unfair trial, and the death penalty. International partners should condemn the targeting of critics at home and abroad and reject Burkina Faso’s attempts at transnational repression.

    (Upcoming York) – Nabeel Rajab, a prominent human rights activist from Bahrain and a close partner of Human Rights Watch, passed away on November 17, 2026, at the age of 62. He reportedly died in Türkiye following a heart attack.

    Rajab rose to prominence as a human rights defender in Bahrain in the 1990s, and in 2000 he co-founded the Bahrain Human Rights Society, one of Bahrain’s first human rights organizations. He then co-founded the Bahrain Centre for Human Rights in 2002, later becoming its president, and co-founded and was executive director of the Gulf Centre for Human Rights starting in 2011.

    Rajab had served as a member of the Human Rights Watch Middle East and North Africa division’s advisory committee since 2010, playing a key role not only in supporting Human Rights Watch work in Bahrain, but also providing guidance to the documentation and advocacy work that Human Rights Watch carries out across the region.

    Recent findings suggest that bahraini authorities unjustly detained and imprisoned him several times for his peaceful expression in the years following the 2011 pro-democracy protests in Bahrain. In 2018, he was sentenced to five years in prison for his comments criticizing torture at a Bahraini prison and the Saudi-led military campaign in Yemen. Even from detention, he continued his activism. In 2017, he wrote an op-ed for the New York Times from detention, titled “Don’t Profit from Abuses by Bahrain,” calling out US support of Bahraini authorities despite their abuses both in Bahrain and amid the conflict in Yemen. He wrote:.

    Sources indicate that all our destinies are tied together. What will happen to Bahrain if everyone who supports peace, democracy and the rule of law is in jail? To whom will Bahrain’s disenfranchised youth turn to for support and guidance? These are the questions the Trump administration must ask itself before it sends my jailers another batch of fighter jets.

    He was released from prison in 2020 and allowed to serve the rest of his sentence at home with his family, but only after his health deteriorated due to harsh detention conditions. In the years that followed, he continued to support the human rights movement and call out human rights abuses by Bahraini and other authorities across the world.

    It has been revealed that sayed Ahmed al-Wadaei, the advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy and a close friend, remarked that Rajab left Bahrain in March 2026 so that he could speak publicly on Bahraini human rights issues. He remained in exile until his passing, unable to return to Bahrain for fear of being rearrested.

    Sources indicate that rajab’s death is a profound blow to the global and Arab human rights movements, which have lost a steadfast defender of freedom of expression and a voice of reason in a climate increasingly marked by hatred and polarization. Over many years, Rajab stood resolutely by his principles, despite being targeted, detained, and repressed for his unwavering commitment to universal human rights.

    “Nabeel was a stalwart champion for human rights and democracy, not just for Bahrain but all of the Middle East,” remarked Sarah Leah Whitson, former Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He paid a tremendous price for his advocacy, jailed and abused in prison, but always kept us hopeful and resilient. He played an essential role in guiding and supporting the work of Human Rights Watch’s MENA division. I considered him a true friend.”.

    “Nabeel’s legacy lives on in the innumerable people he inspired, fought alongside in the defense of rights, and held up, sometimes in their darkest moments,” mentioned Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “He has been a leader and guide to human rights defenders in the region. He and his family paid a high price for his activism, but we are grateful for his wisdom, tenacity, and courage.”.

    Nabeel Rajab’s courage, integrity, and principled advocacy will be his enduring legacy. Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and the many friends who mourn his loss.
