    We’re looking for a Product Manager, Administration & Governance to join our Product Team and make Supabase the default starting point for software built inside a firm.

    Sources indicate that supabase already spreads from the bottom up: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. Inside most companies, Supabase starts the same way: someone has an idea, creates a project, and builds something useful. The next step is making that momentum company-wide: one platform where anyone can start building, and where IT can see what’s running, who owns it, and what it costs.

    You’ll own how companies run Supabase as their internal development platform: approved by IT and easy for anyone in the tech giant to use. You’ll make it possible for people and the agents they work with to start building without waiting on infrastructure, while giving platform, IT, and security teams the controls they need to say yes. The goal is to make the approved path the easiest path, from an early experiment to a production application, with the controls companies need built in.

    Own the product strategy and roadmap for internal innovation, from a tech giant’s first IT-approved rollout to adoption across teams and business units.

    Make getting started self-service, whether someone creates a project in Supabase, through an internal developer portal, or with an agent. Give builders the access and infrastructure they need without a ticket for every project.

    Steer scattered usage into a manageable company-wide platform. Give companies one view of everything they run on Supabase. Shape how ownership, delegated access, and boundaries work so teams can move independently as usage grows.

    According to recent reports, partner closely with platform, IT, security, and finance teams to understand what it takes to approve Supabase and keep it approved. Translate their needs into practical identity, policy, audit, and spend controls that don’t slow builders down.

    Define the path from experiment to production, including project ownership, access, and the guardrails that change as an application becomes notable to the business.

    Work with Engineering, Design, Sales, and Customer Success to turn early customer rollouts into a repeatable experience, rather than a new custom integration for every tech giant.

    Define what success looks like, instrument it end to end, and let the data guide what gets built next—from time to first project and self-service adoption to production usage and expansion across the organization.

    Have 7+ years of product management on developer tools, infrastructure, or internal developer platforms.

    Have built self-service products that developers love and platform or IT teams trust. You understand both the person trying to ship an app and the team responsible for how it runs.

    Can reason about identity, permissions, organization boundaries, and usage attribution, and turn those systems into workflows people can actually understand.

    Have a strong point of view on how agents change who can build software inside a tech giant and what an internal development platform needs to make that possible.

    Know your way around controlled experimentation and data analysis, and can connect easier adoption to sustained product use.

    Are biased toward speed and would rather ship, learn, and iterate than perfect a spec.

    Build with what you own and form opinions through first-hand use, from creating a project to configuring the policies around it.

    Use AI tools to compress research, drafting, and feedback synthesis so you can focus on judgment calls.

    Work async by default, making decisions in writing in a fully remote team.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Sources indicate that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    Recent findings suggest that once a year, the entire company gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    In a recent development, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #181562. Marisa de los Santos on John Green, detectives, and switching genres as a writer

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1538 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Marisa de los Santos on John Green, detectives, and switching genres as a writer

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • John Green wrote this: “I fell asleep the way you fall in love, slowly and then all at once.”.
    • According to recent reports, I treasure this quotation because it applies to so many changes and revelations, and it happens to be a really good description of how I fell into writing crime fiction.
    • I’ve wanted to write detective fiction for a very long time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    John Green wrote this: “I fell asleep the way you fall in love, slowly and then all at once.”.

    According to recent reports, I treasure this quotation because it applies to so many changes and revelations, and it happens to be a really good description of how I fell into writing crime fiction. After a career built mostly on upmarket fiction or women’s fiction or book club fiction or whatever term is meant to describe books mostly about relationships, mostly by women, I’ve switched genres. Forever? Not sure. For now? Absolutely. Does it feel momentous? Kind of, yes. How did it happen? Slowly and then all at once.

    I’ve wanted to write detective fiction for a very long time. Years. As a reader, I devour it. For well over a decade, when someone asked me to list my favorite living writers, Tana French was one of the first names out of my mouth. She still is. In my mind, she’s the gold standard, but there are many other crime writers on the list, writers of the kind of book you read and immediately say, “God, I wish I’d written that.”.

    Why? When I think about this question, I run into that thing where you try to explain why you love something that feels so natural and second nature to love that you’re at a loss. It must be due in part to the way I’m fascinated by puzzles: word, jigsaw, logic, riddles, any knotty problem that doesn’t have to do with numbers.

    Sources indicate that I’m drawn to intricately put-together things that also seem seamless. Poetry is like that, which is maybe why I started out as a poet. There’s a mystery at the heart of every good poem, a thing to unlock, language that flings open a window to a fresh view of what it is to be a person in the world. The tangled and cryptic made beautifully or tragically or terrifyingly clear.

    Sources indicate that also, I love crime fiction for the way it can mop its characters into the darkest corners and then force them to find their way out. Characters in detective fiction confront humanity at its most broken, and sometimes that humanity is their own.

    It has been revealed that I’m especially fascinated by the perspective of the detectives, people whose life’s work is predicated on people hurting other people, whether it’s out of fear, jealousy, personal gain, desperation, or what can only be called evil. Imagine making a pact with the world to stare down what most of us try to avoid, evil and destruction, and to try to hold to account the people who have the audacity to hurt, to murder their fellow human beings.

    Detectives pick a side in a way that most of us never have to and they do their best to keep their feet firmly planted on the ground of right and just, even when that ground shakes under them.

    So why didn’t I write a crime novel ages ago? There are two reasons.

    Recent findings suggest that firstly, I’ve never had a lot of choice about what I write. I’ve never been a writer with loads of book ideas or one that states, with deliberation, “I want to write X next.” There’s usually a single idea that comes out of the kind of nowhere that’s really everywhere: newspapers, encounters on the street, an overheard conversation, a weirdly blue sky or the way the light hits someone’s face. So many tiny glimmers and slivers that eventually coalesce into an idea.

    It has been revealed that I write what I’m given to write. I hate how woo-woo that sounds, but oh well. That’s the way it is.

    And secondly, I didn’t have a character. Nearly everything I’ve ever written begins with a character, one that lives and develops inside my head, sometimes for years. For me, the story emerges from the characters, not the other way around. And for a long time, I didn’t have a detective character, even though I really, really wanted one.

    But to get to the “slowly” part from the John Green quotation, when I look at my books that weren’t mysteries, I see that they were. There’s a mystery at the center of each of them and, in some of them, there’s a character who is actively seeking to solve that mystery.

    In a recent development, A boy looking for his biological father. A young woman trying to discover the history of the house she’s inherited. A woman seeking out, however reluctantly, the person who set a fire that threw her world into heartbreak. Two sisters trying to uncover lost years of their mother’s life before it’s too late.

    Detectives who aren’t detectives. Mysteries that aren’t murders. Clues to follow. Red herrings. Scraps and shards and dark corners and someone taking the measure of human cruelty or courage or grief or love and picking a side.

    According to recent reports, which brings us to the “all at once” part: Lina Cordova. My detective. Well, one of two. Aaron Cash would show up a little later (God, I love that guy). But Lina came first. She arrived suddenly and then lived inside my head until she became a full-fledged person to me. Where did she come from? Beats me. Why then and not before? No idea. But I was super happy to see her.

    Lina is half-Filipina, half-white, like me. She has a Filipino doctor father, like me. She is fiercely in love with her people, her dogs, her home. So am I. But she’s not me. She’s way taller, for one thing. And worlds braver. I learned her like you learn a language, slowly then all at once. Before I could write her story, I had to become Lina-fluent. So that’s what I did. It was awesome.

    She had the same best friend, Helly, from childhood, through elementary, middle, high school, through college and Lina’s law school years, and into adulthood. Then, someone murdered Helly and that person was never held to account and Lina’s heart and her whole being cracked.

    Recent findings suggest that for a long time, she lost herself. So, as so many of us do, she took her shattered self and her family home, to the small city of Sheppley, Pennsylvania, where she found herself again, and she became a cop. One whose ace in the hole is her dead best friend, the voice inside her head that pushes her, sometimes relentlessly, toward the truth. Lina talks to Helly and Helly talks back and of course it’s not really Helly, but, for Lina, it is.

    Lina is a mother. She has a teenage daughter and a son on the autism spectrum. She has an ex-husband named Joe, who is still her safe harbor in every storm. She has a dead mother she adores and a father with whom she and her kids live and who is grumpy and bossy and as solid as a lighthouse on a rock. She is drawn to pretty clothes and excellent coffee. She comes home each day to an old stone house, warm yellow light, kids doing homework, two Yorkies, the smell of her dad’s cooking, and peace.

    Recent findings suggest that I like an edgy, brooding, jaded, teetering-on-the edge-of-some-personal-chasm-or-other detective as much as the next person, but that’s not Lina. (It’s not Aaron, either, despite his past, the sort people are lucky to get out of alive).

    In a recent development, lina has her frailties: at one point, she calls herself a “soft-boiled detective” and she’s right. No emotional armor, no cynicism. She can’t help but think of even the worst criminals as not monsters but human, a fact that can make her job extremely hard and that also functions as her superpower. She’s the kind of person who watches a pregnant fox cross a road in front of her and feels so protective of it she could weep. She’s funny and piercingly smart. She is haunted, hunted like a fox by hounds, by the cases she left unsolved.

    All at once, I had Lina. And then, I had Aaron. And then, from these two people, all at once, I had The Trusted. Because in that way the world of crime fiction is like the world of any other fiction, at least for me, a place where the story emerges from the characters, spins itself into being out of who they are: their personal histories, all their little quirks and preferences and weirdness, their friendships, all their passions, the books they read, the food they eat, everything that scares or sustains them.

    Recent findings suggest that thanks for showing up, Lina. You, too, Aaron. Thank you to all my earlier books and the characters who allowed them to happen. It turns out, at long last, slowly then all at once, I got to be a crime writer after all.

    Marisa de los Santos is the Latest York Times bestselling author of Love Walked In, Belong to Me, The Trusted, and Falling Together. She has also published a poetry collection called From the Bones Out.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, was sentenced today to 18 years in prison and lifetime supervised release by U.S. District Judge David C. Nye of the District of Idaho for attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

    According to recent reports, according to court records, Mercurio planned to incapacitate his father with a metal pipe and take his firearms to use in a mass casualty attack on Idaho churches in the name of ISIS. Mercurio also planned to use flame-covered weapons, explosives, knives, and a machete in the attacks. A search of his house revealed that he had butane canisters, lighters, a pair of handcuffs, a knife, and a machete, as well as several firearms belonging to his father. Days before the planned attack, Mercurio stood before an ISIS flag holding a knife and pledged his allegiance to ISIS. The FBI arrested him on April 6, 2024, one day before his planned attack. In addition to his plot to attack Idaho churches, in early 2023, he created an online repository for pro-ISIS content with the purpose of spreading the doctrine of the Islamic State.

    “America’s founders wanted our Nation to be a place where the faithful of any denomination could exercise their religious beliefs freely and without fear of violence,” mentioned Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Alexander Scott Mercurio planned to attack that fundamental freedom by bringing death and destruction to several churches. This sentence highlights that the Department of Justice will relentlessly investigate, pursue, and prosecute those who would terrorize and murder Americans for exercising their religious rights.”.

    “The sentencing of Mercurio today sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States – whether in Coeur d’Alene, or any other community – they will be brought to justice,” remarked U.S. Attorney John C. Shirts for the District of Idaho. “Protecting our communities from terrorist activity is always the number one priority of this office and the Department of Justice. I commend the investigation by the FBI, as well as the valuable assistance provided by the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.”.

    “With today’s sentencing, this individual is being held accountable for pledging allegiance to ISIS and planning an attack on U.S. soil,” mentioned Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI works tirelessly to detect and prevent acts of terrorism in order to protect the American people. We will continue to work closely with our law enforcement and Justice Department partners to make sure anyone who participates in terrorist acts faces justice.”.

    The case was investigated by the FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force with assistance from the Coeur d’Alene Police Department, the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office and the Ada County Sheriff’s Office.

    It has been revealed that the case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Heather S. Patricco and David G. Robins for the District of Idaho and Trial Attorney Matthew R. Hracho of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.
